feed.title: Flock in Owens Valley, California

image.credit: Ansel Adams, U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams made this photograph of a flock of sheep in Owens Valley, California, in 1941. It belongs to the series Ansel Adams Photographs of National Parks and Monuments, compiled in 1941 and 1942. He was an American landscape photographer and environmentalist, known for his black-and-white images of the American West. He helped found Group f/64, which favoured sharp focus and the full tonal range of a photograph, and developed the Zone System with Fred Archer, a method for reaching a desired print through choices in exposure, development and printing. He was later contracted by the United States Department of the Interior to photograph national parks. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1980.
feed.lookAt: The sheep walk in a loose line toward the right while dust hangs over the flat ground, and a ridge of distant peaks closes the top. Adams placed the animals in the lower third and gave the land and sky the rest. Include the setting around the subject, not just the subject.

feed.title: El Tatio geyser field

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: El Tatio is a geothermal field in the Andes of northern Chile, at 4,320 metres above sea level. It is the third-largest geyser field in the world and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere, with more than 80 active geysers. It lies at the western foot of a line of stratovolcanoes along the border between Chile and Bolivia, and water from its hot springs eventually forms the Rio Salado, a tributary of the Rio Loa. It is a major tourism destination, and has been studied as an analogue for the early Earth. This close-up of a geyser was taken on 1 February 2016, with steam drifting across the plain behind a mound of mineral deposits.
feed.lookAt: Steam turns the air into a soft screen that thickens with distance, separating the pale mound in front from the faint hills behind. Low light at either end of the day makes that depth visible. Put the solid subject in the foreground and let the vapour do the layering.

feed.title: Dynjandi

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Dynjandi, also known as Fjallfoss, is a waterfall in Arnarfjörður in the Westfjords region of Iceland. It is the largest waterfall in the Westfjords and has a total height of 100 metres. Below it lie five other waterfalls: Háifoss, Úðafoss, Göngufoss, Hundafoss and Bæjarfoss. Dynjandi and the other falls on the river Dynjandisá, along with their surroundings, were protected as natural monuments in 1981. Dynjandisheiði, a mountain pass over the falls, holds the first car-accessible road to Ísafjörður. This photograph was taken on 14 August 2014. It is a combination of several exposures, with the lower fall softened into a smooth white veil.
feed.lookAt: Two kinds of water share this frame. The upper fall keeps its texture and the lower one is blurred into silk, which points to a slower shutter on a tripod. Choose the shutter speed for the effect you want, and let wet rock and moss in the foreground add contrast.

feed.title: Frozen Lake and Cliffs, Sierra Nevada

image.credit: Ansel Adams, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams took Frozen Lake and Cliffs, Sierra Nevada, California, in 1927, and it was published in 1932. Adams was an American landscape photographer and environmentalist, who at age 14 was given his first camera during his first visit to Yosemite National Park. He developed his early photographic work as a member of the Sierra Club. He later helped found Group f/64, an association of photographers advocating pure photography that favoured sharp focus and the full tonal range, and with Fred Archer he developed the Zone System. He was a life-long advocate of environmental conservation, and his work was deeply entwined with that advocacy. In 1980 he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his work and persistent advocacy.
feed.lookAt: Black rock, white ice and dark water form a strip of tones that runs across the frame, and the cliff keeps fine detail even in its shadows. Take a reading from both the brightest and darkest parts, then choose an exposure that holds both.

caption.title: Frozen Lake and Cliffs, Sierra Nevada

feed.title: Inspiration Point, Bryce Canyon

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Bryce Canyon is not a true canyon but a collection of giant natural amphitheaters along the eastern side of the Paunsaugunt Plateau in southwestern Utah. Its distinctive hoodoos were formed by frost weathering and stream erosion of river and lake bed sedimentary rock, and the red, orange and white colours of the stone give the park its look. The area was settled by Mormon pioneers in the 1850s and named after Ebenezer Bryce, who homesteaded there in 1874. It became a national monument in 1923 and a national park in 1928. This four-segment panorama of Inspiration Point was taken on 20 November 2018 at 08:15, in early morning light.
feed.lookAt: Morning sun lights the hoodoos from the side, so every spire throws a shadow and the amphitheater gains depth. The curving trail on the right leads the eye toward the far ridge. When the subject is too wide for one frame, stitch a panorama and keep the horizon level.

feed.title: Namib-Naukluft dunes

image.credit: Yathin S Krishnappa, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Namib-Naukluft National Park lies in western Namibia between the Atlantic coast and the edge of the Great Escarpment. It covers part of the Namib Desert, which is considered the world's oldest desert, along with the Naukluft mountain range and the lagoon at Sandwich Harbour. Its best-known area, and one of the main visitor attractions in Namibia, is Sossusvlei, a clay pan surrounded by dunes. The file description notes that the older dunes are reddish and larger, while the newer dunes are yellow-brown. This photograph was taken on 20 April 2011 at 07:52 in the morning, when low sun lit only parts of the dune faces.
feed.lookAt: Early sun lights some dune slopes orange while others fall into shadow, so the frame splits into bands of colour. A single small tree at the bottom edge shows the scale. Use a long lens to flatten the dunes into layers, and wait for the light to sweep across.

feed.title: Santa Fe railroad yard, Los Angeles

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano made this colour transparency in March 1943 in the Santa Fe Railroad yard in Los Angeles. The Library of Congress title records that all switch lights, headlights and lamps had been shaded from above in accordance with blackout regulations. The heavy streaks of light were caused by the paths of locomotive headlights, and the thin lines by the lamps of switchmen working in the yard. Delano was born Yakov Ovcharov in the Russian Empire and spent much of his life in Puerto Rico. In the United States he worked for the Farm Security Administration, for which he was best known. He was also a composer, filmmaker, cartoonist and poet.
feed.lookAt: Nothing in the yard is still, so the lights draw their own paths: fat streaks from locomotives, thin wavy lines from walking switchmen. Delano left the shutter open. Put the camera on a firm support at night, and let moving lights write across a dark scene.

caption.title: Santa Fe railroad yard, Los Angeles

feed.title: Grose Valley

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Grose Valley is a rugged valley in the Blue Mountains of New South Wales, formed by the Grose River. Most of it lies within Blue Mountains National Park, between the Great Western Highway and Bells Line of Road. Triassic sandstones sit over Permian sedimentary rocks, and the cliffs are commonly over 200 metres, rising to 510 metres at Banks Wall. Charles Darwin called it stupendous and magnificent when he visited in 1836. In 1931 and 1932 a Sydney Bush Walkers group saved Blue Gum Forest from clearing by raising £130 to buy out a lease. This panorama, stitched from two rows of nine frames, was taken on 14 April 2013 from Rodreguez Pass near Govett's Leap.
feed.lookAt: A clear blue sky and sharp cliffs give a crisp, high-contrast scene. The sandstone wall on the right anchors the frame and the valley recedes in overlapping ridges to the left. A panorama like this works best when you step back from the edge and include foreground trees for scale.

feed.title: Geirangerfjord

image.credit: Simo Räsänen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Geirangerfjord is a fjord in the Sunnmøre region of Møre og Romsdal county, Norway, lying entirely within Stranda Municipality. It is a branch of the Sunnylvsfjorden, which itself branches off the Storfjorden, and it runs about 15 kilometres with a maximum width of 1.5 kilometres. The village of Geiranger sits at its end, where the river Geirangelva meets the water. The fjord was inscribed in 2005, jointly with Nærøyfjord, as the West Norwegian Fjords World Heritage Site, and it is among the most visited tourist sites in Norway. This view was taken on 16 June 2013 from Ørnesvingen, looking down onto the green slopes and dark water below.
feed.lookAt: Shooting from a high bend in the road lets the fjord curl through the frame like a river of dark glass. The bright foliage in the foreground frames both sides, and the steep slopes keep the eye moving. Seek elevation to turn water and shoreline into a shape.

feed.title: Hulett unloaders, Cleveland ore docks

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano made this colour transparency in May 1943 at the Pennsylvania Railroad ore docks in Cleveland, Ohio. The Library of Congress title describes iron ore being unloaded from a lake freighter by means of Hulett unloaders. Delano was born Yakov Ovcharov in the Russian Empire and spent much of his life in Puerto Rico. In the United States he worked for the Works Progress Administration and, most notably, the Farm Security Administration. He was a photographer, filmmaker and composer who also worked as a cartoonist, poet, professor and architectural designer. The picture records wartime industry at a working freight dock.
feed.lookAt: Heavy steel arms cut across the sky in strong diagonals, while the numbered hatches of the freighter run toward the vanishing point. Delano stood on the ship's deck to get both. Look for converging lines in industrial structures, and use a small figure to show the scale.

feed.title: Brihadisvara Temple

image.credit: Rainer Halama, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Thanjavur, south bank of the Cauvery

feed.story: Brihadisvara Temple, called Rajarajesvaram by its builder and known locally as Thanjai Periya Kovil, stands on the south bank of the Cauvery river in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. The Chola emperor Rajaraja I built it between 1003 and 1010 CE. It is one of the largest Hindu temples and an exemplar of Tamil architecture, and it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the Great Living Chola Temples. It is built of granite, and its vimana tower is one of the tallest in South India. This photograph was taken at 19:46 on 27 February 2025, during Maha Shivaratri, as the temple glowed under the dusk sky.
feed.lookAt: The sky has gone deep blue but still holds a band of pink, and the lit temple glows against it. Shooting in that short window after sunset balances artificial lights with the last daylight. Use a tripod and expose for the sky, so the lamps do not blow out.

feed.title: Bayon, Angkor Thom

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Bayon is a richly decorated Buddhist temple of the Khmer Empire at Angkor in Cambodia. It was built in the late 12th or early 13th century as the state temple of King Jayavarman VII, at the centre of his capital, Angkor Thom. It is best known for its many towers carved with serene, smiling stone faces on all sides, commonly interpreted as representations of the king and symbols of compassion. Extensive bas-reliefs depict historical events, religious themes and scenes of everyday life, making it an important visual source on Angkorian society. This photograph was taken at 15:17 on 17 August 2013, with a still green pond in the foreground.
feed.lookAt: The temple is set in a wide, low frame with the towers rising from the middle, and the still, green pond in the foreground fills the lower third. Standing back from the subject shows its outline at once. Keep the horizon level and let the ground carry the scale of the ruin.

feed.title: Lincoln Memorial and Reflecting Pool from the Washington Monument

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith photographed the Lincoln Memorial, the Reflecting Pool and the World War II Memorial from the Washington Monument at 10:06 on 19 September 2010. The image belongs to the George F. Landegger Collection of District of Columbia Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America at the Library of Congress. Highsmith began her nationwide photography project after extensively photographing the Willard Hotel in the early 1980s for its restoration. She has donated her photographs to the Library of Congress since 1992, creating a collection of nearly 100,000 images, all in the public domain. Her work documents the landscapes, architecture and people of the rural and urban United States.
feed.lookAt: From a great height the Mall becomes a straight axis, with the pool as a long mirror leading to the memorial. A slight haze softens the far skyline. High vantage points reveal the plan of a place: find the line that organises it and place it at the centre.

caption.title: Lincoln Memorial and Reflecting Pool from the Washington Monument
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Phaung Daw U Pagoda, Meiktila

image.credit: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Meiktila is a city in central Myanmar, on the banks of Meiktila Lake in the Mandalay Region, at the junction of the Bagan–Taunggyi, Yangon–Mandalay and Meiktila–Myingyan highways. The lake is an artificial irrigation and water reservoir about 11 kilometres long, and the best-known of the city's 44 Buddhist pagodas, as of 2020, are on its lakefront. The name comes from Mithila, an ancient Indian kingdom. Meiktila was also the site of the Battle of Meiktila and Mandalay, in which Allied forces under William Slim defeated Japanese forces. This photograph shows the Phaung Daw U Pagoda at 16:20 on 3 August 2016, under a blue sky with scattered cloud.
feed.lookAt: The golden bird's head crosses into the sky on the right and the long barge recedes to the left, so a diagonal leads you through the picture. Clouds add texture to the blue behind it. Wait for the sky to open up, and place the brightest shape against the cleanest background.

feed.title: St. Mary's Church, Negombo

image.credit: Steffen Schmitz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: St. Mary's Church is a Roman Catholic church on Grand Street in the heart of Negombo, and one of the largest Catholic churches in Sri Lanka. The first church on the site was established in 1544, and the present building, the fifth, was begun in 1874 and completed in 1922. It is neoclassical, with columns and plain walls. Inside, the ceilings are painted with scenes from the life of Christ by N. S. Godamanne, a local Buddhist painter, and the article describes the art and architecture as a blend of European practice with Sri Lankan art. Negombo is nicknamed Little Rome because of its many churches. This photograph was taken on 15 July 2025.
feed.lookAt: The church is shot square on from the middle of the road, so its two towers, pediment and columns mirror each other on both sides. Direct, even light keeps the pink and grey tones clean. Symmetry rewards a centred position, but check that the verticals stay straight.

feed.title: Nightview, New York

image.credit: Berenice Abbott, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Berenice Abbott made this nighttime view of Midtown Manhattan from the top of the Empire State Building. Sources give dates ranging from 1930 to 1934. Abbott was an American photographer best known for her portraits of cultural figures of the interwar period, for her photographs of New York's architecture and urban design in the 1930s, and for science interpretation in the 1940s to the 1960s. In the early 1940s she developed Super Sight, also known as the Abbott Process, a form of macro photography. Because the file's source dates vary, the exact year of this photograph is uncertain.
feed.lookAt: The city is a field of small lit windows, with an elevated railway line cutting across the lower right as the single diagonal. Looking down from a great height flattens the buildings into pattern. Use a tripod at night, and let the lit windows carry the texture.

feed.title: Gandhi Bhawan, Chandigarh

image.credit: UnpetitproleX, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: B. P. Mathur with Pierre Jeanneret

feed.story: Gandhi Bhawan is a major landmark of Chandigarh, India, and a centre dedicated to the study of the words and works of Mohandas K. Gandhi. It was designed by the architect B. P. Mathur in collaboration with Pierre Jeanneret. The building stands on a raised plinth in a large pool, with an angular and curved three-part pinwheel roof meant to evoke a floating lotus flower. Its white colour was chosen to contrast with the red of the Fine Arts Museum designed by Le Corbusier, visible on the right of this frame. The photograph was taken on 26 September 2024, after an intense thunderstorm, when the pool lay still.
feed.lookAt: After the storm the pool is flat enough to hold a near-perfect reflection, which doubles the angular roof into a diamond. The red wall on the right sets off the white concrete. Shoot low to the water and wait for the surface to settle.

feed.title: Parkview Square

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Parkview Square is an office building in the Downtown Core of Singapore, along North Bridge Road near Bugis. Construction began in 1999 and it was completed in 2002. It rises 144 metres across 24 floors, and was designed by the American architect James Adams with DP Architects of Singapore as local architect. Although it is a modern building, it is designed in a classic Art Deco style inspired by New York's Chanin Building of 1929. In this photograph, taken from Rochor Road at 17:00 on 12 June 2018, it stands beside the glass Andaz hotel building.
feed.lookAt: Two towers face each other: bronze-toned Art Deco on the left, glass and plants on the right. The contrast between ornament and grid is the picture. Pick a spot where two different styles meet, and keep the verticals straight so the cliff of each wall holds.

feed.title: Stone and William Street, Manhattan

image.credit: Berenice Abbott, New York Public Library, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Berenice Abbott photographed the corner of Stone and William Street in Manhattan on 12 May 1936. The New York Public Library's note describes the view as looking up at an inter-building bridge, with the buildings in the foreground as dark masses and the buildings beyond well lit. Abbott was an American photographer best known for her portraits of cultural figures of the interwar period and for her photographs of the architecture and urban design of New York in the 1930s. In the early 1940s she also developed Super Sight, also known as the Abbott Process, a form of macro photography. This print is catalogued by the library under the reference CNY number 116.
feed.lookAt: Tilting the camera upward makes the towers lean in and the sky a narrow gap, while the footbridge floats across the middle. Dark foreground walls act as a frame around the light buildings. Point up, include a frame within a frame, and keep dark masses to push the bright ones forward.

caption.line2: Berenice Abbott · New York Public Library

feed.title: Piazzetta San Marco, Venice

image.credit: Benh Lieu Song, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Venice is a coastal city in northeastern Italy, built on a group of 126 islands separated by canals and linked in part by 472 bridges. It was the capital of the Republic of Venice for almost a millennium, from 810 to 1797, and a major financial and maritime power in the Middle Ages and Renaissance. This view of the Piazzetta San Marco looks toward the Grand Canal at dawn, with the Doge's Palace on the left and the Biblioteca Marciana on the right. The two columns, Saint Mark's, protector of the city, on one and Saint Theodore's on the other, stand at the water's edge. The photograph was taken on 10 July 2015.
feed.lookAt: Blue-hour light is balanced between sky and street lamps, and the wet pavement echoes the glow. The two arcades run in toward the columns like a pair of guide rails. Get there before the crowds and use a tripod, so the empty square is part of the picture.

feed.title: Centre Block, Parliament Hill

image.credit: Saffron Blaze, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Centre Block is the main building of the Canadian Parliament on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario, and holds the House of Commons and Senate chambers. It is built in the Gothic Revival style and is the building's second version: the first was destroyed by a fire in 1916, and only the Library of Parliament at the rear survives from it. Sculpting work on the interior continued into the 1970s. From 2018, members of Parliament were moved elsewhere for renovations lasting until 2031. The Peace Tower is shown on the Canadian $20 bill. This photograph, taken at 17:52 on 24 September 2013, shows the front under a clear blue sky.
feed.lookAt: The tower stands on the exact centre line and the two wings repeat evenly on each side. A cloudless deep-blue sky lifts the stone and the copper spire. Formal subjects reward a dead-centre view, a level horizon and a slightly longer lens, so the lines do not lean.

feed.title: Times Square on a rainy day

image.credit: John Vachon, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: John Vachon photographed Times Square in New York City on a rainy day in March 1943, between 2 and 17 March according to the file page. Vachon was an American photographer, remembered most for his work for the Farm Security Administration as part of the New Deal, and for his contributions to Look magazine. He was born in 1914 and died in 1975. The picture shows the wet street, the signs of Globe and others, and a bus at the right edge. It records the city during wartime, in grey weather. Only the month and range of days are known from the file; no other details of the commission are given there.
feed.lookAt: Rain turns the street into a mirror, and the grey sky keeps the contrast soft enough to show detail in the signs. A man and a woman with an umbrella stand in the middle distance and give the scene human scale. Wet days reward waiting for a figure to enter the frame.

caption.title: Times Square on a rainy day

feed.title: Teatro del Lago, Frutillar

image.credit: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Teatro del Lago is a concert hall on the shore of Llanquihue Lake in Frutillar, in Chile's Los Lagos Region. Gerardo Köster and Gustavo Greene began construction in 1998, and in 2008 a second team from Amercanda joined to use better acoustic materials. After about twelve years of work and a cost of US$20 million, it opened on 6 November 2010. The main concert hall holds 1,178 people, and a separate amphitheater seats 270. The theatre hosts the Semanas Musicales de Frutillar, Chile's biggest classical music festival, each late January and early February. This photograph was taken on 8 May 2011, with a snow-capped peak on the far horizon.
feed.lookAt: The wooden building leads from the right toward the lake and a distant white-capped peak, so a single frame holds architecture, water and mountain. The low sun warms the timber. Include a far landmark to place the building, and keep the people small for scale.

feed.title: Clevedon Pier

image.credit: Saffron Blaze, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Clevedon Pier is a seaside pier in Clevedon, Somerset, on the east shore of the Severn Estuary. Sir John Betjeman called it the most beautiful pier in England, and it was made a Grade I listed building in 2001. It was built in the 1860s to attract tourists and provide a ferry port for rail passengers going to South Wales, and it opened in 1869. It is 312 metres long, with eight spans. Two of those spans collapsed during stress testing in 1970, and local fundraising and heritage grants allowed the pier to be dismantled, restored and reassembled. It fully reopened in 1998. This photograph was taken on 7 July 2013 at 22:15.
feed.lookAt: The sun has just gone, and orange sky and calm water fuse into one glowing field. The pier runs across the frame as a dark line, its arches repeating in reflection. A long exposure smooths the surface; set the horizon high or low, never in the middle.

feed.title: A boat on a river, China

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein photographed a boat on a river with rolling hills in the background in 1946, in the Jiangsu Province or Yunnan Province of China; the file does not say which. Rothstein was an American photographer whose career spanned five decades, and he received recognition as one of America's premier photojournalists. He was born in 1915 and died in 1985. This picture shows a sailing junk with patched sails on calm water, the hills behind it, and the boat and its reflection in the river. The file gives only the year and the description, so details of the commission and of the exact location are not stated here.
feed.lookAt: A single dark boat sits on the right third, its patched sail and reflection making a vertical against the long horizontal of the water. The hills run in a low band behind. Keep the subject off centre, and leave open water on the side it faces.

caption.title: A boat on a river, China

feed.title: Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng National Park

image.credit: Tycho, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng is a national park and UNESCO World Heritage Site in central Quảng Trị Province, about 500 km south of Hanoi. It sits on a limestone zone of 2,000 km² that borders Hin Namno National Park in Laos. The park was created to protect one of the world's two largest karst regions, with 300 caves and grottoes. A 2009 survey brought the total discovered length of the cave system to about 126 km, and many areas are still unexplored. Sơn Đoòng Cave, found in that survey, is considered the largest cave in the world. This photograph of one of the park's caves was taken on 12 November 2012; the file does not name the cave.
feed.lookAt: A lamp lights the pale, folded rock walls in yellow and green, while the arched opening at the centre stays dark with a faint green glow beyond. Light one side of a cave and expose for it; let the far distance fall to shadow, so the dark arch gives depth.

feed.title: Phnom Bakheng

image.credit: Satdeep Gill, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Phnom Bakheng is a Buddhist temple in the form of a temple mountain at Angkor, in Siem Reap Province, Cambodia. It was originally a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva and was built at the end of the 9th century, in the reign of King Yasovarman. It stands on a hill and is now a popular spot for sunset views of Angkor Wat, which lies about 1.5 km to the southeast. The many visitors make it one of the most threatened monuments at Angkor. Since 2004 the World Monuments Fund has worked on its conservation with APSARA. This photograph was taken on 9 September 2022.
feed.lookAt: The central shrine fills the frame square on, its carved figures in niches either side of a doorway that opens onto a darker room and a gap of light beyond. Stand on the axis of a symmetrical building and let the door act as an inner frame.

feed.title: The Ellipse from the Washington Monument

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith photographed the Ellipse, the oval lawn south of the White House, from the Washington Monument on 19 September 2010. The Library of Congress title is View of the Ellipse, from the Washington Monument, NW, Washington, D.C., and the title, date and subject note were provided by the photographer. The picture belongs to the George F. Landegger Collection of District of Columbia Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, a gift to the Library of Congress in 2010. Highsmith is an American photographer whose nationwide study of the country's landscapes, architecture and people has run since the 1980s. Her photographs are all in the public domain.
feed.lookAt: Seen from the monument's height, the oval lawn sits in the left foreground, ringed by trees, while avenues run straight toward a distant horizon between blocks of city buildings. A thin band of cloud crosses the sky. Use an elevated view to show how a city is planned.

caption.title: The Ellipse from the Washington Monument
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Mường Thanh Valley

image.credit: Tycho, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Mường Thanh Valley lies in Điện Biên Province in northwestern Vietnam. It is about 20 km long and 5 km wide, a heart-shaped basin ringed by jungle, rice paddies and lakes. The city of Điện Biên Phủ stands within it. As the provincial capital, Điện Biên Phủ is famous as the site of a decisive battle in 1954, in which French forces were defeated by Việt Minh troops under General Võ Nguyên Giáp. This photograph, taken from the city at 07:30 on 9 November 2012, looks across the valley's wooded edge to the ridges beyond.
feed.lookAt: Shafts of sunlight break through a dark cloud ceiling and fan across layered, hazy ridges, while the rooftops below sit in shade. Wait for gaps in heavy cloud; expose for the bright sky so the beams read clearly, and let the foreground go dark.

feed.title: Petronas Towers

image.credit: Dcubillas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Petronas Towers are an interlinked pair of 88-storey supertall skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, standing 451.9 m high. From 1998 to 2004 they were the tallest buildings in the world, until Taipei 101 in Taiwan surpassed them, and they remain the world's tallest twin skyscrapers. They were the tallest buildings in Malaysia until 2019. This photograph was taken at night on 4 November 2008, from the base of one tower, looking up towards the other. One of the large Malaysian flags on the towers is lit at the bottom centre of the frame.
feed.lookAt: Looking straight up, the towers' steel-and-glass sides converge and curve toward the dark sky, with the bridge crossing between them. A lit flag in the lower left gives a splash of colour and a sense of scale. Tilt up from the base to dramatise height.

feed.title: Freight terminal, Chicago

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano made this colour transparency in April 1943. The Library of Congress title is Trucks unloading at the inbound freight house of the Illinois Central Railroad, South Water Street freight terminal, Chicago, Ill. Delano was born Yakov Ovcharov in the Russian Empire, in 1914, and spent much of his life in Puerto Rico. In the United States he worked for the Works Progress Administration and, most notably, the Farm Security Administration. He was also a composer, a cartoonist, a poet, a professor and an architectural designer. The file gives no more detail about the day or the viewpoint of this particular picture.
feed.lookAt: Rows of red boxcars sit low along the freight house, while tall pale and dark towers stand behind them under a blue sky. The flat yard in the foreground leads to the skyline. Contrast the humble workaday foreground with the grand buildings behind it.

feed.title: Inle Lake

image.credit: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Inle Lake is a freshwater lake in Nyaungshwe Township, Shan State, in the Shan Hills of Myanmar. It is the country's second largest lake, covering about 116 km² at an elevation of 880 m. Its average depth in the dry season is 2.1 m, and it rises by about 1.5 m in the rainy season. Large sections are covered by floating plants, and the clear, slightly alkaline water holds more than 35 native fish species, 17 of them endemic. About 20,000 migratory gulls visit from November to January. This photograph of a fisherman on the lake was taken at 17:01 on 5 August 2016.
feed.lookAt: The fisherman stands upright on a narrow boat, one hand on a long oar, beside a conical net held open on its frame. The net's curved lines fill the right half against green hills. Wait for the pose that tells the story.

feed.title: Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay is a performing arts centre in the Downtown Core of Singapore, near the mouth of the Singapore River. It takes its name from the nearby Esplanade Park. It consists of two rounded structures: one houses a concert hall with about 1,600 seats, and the other a theatre with a capacity of about 2,000. People nickname it The Durian, and the name refers to the nearby Esplanade Park rather than to the building's shape. This photograph was taken at 18:35 on 12 June 2018, at blue hour, with the lit interior glowing through the spiked glass shell.
feed.lookAt: Against a deep blue sky, the glass shell glows warm inside while its spiked frame stays cool and silver. The white support legs and lit base balance the dome. Shoot at blue hour, when sky and building lights are close in brightness.

feed.title: Locomotives in the roundhouse, Proviso yard

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano made this colour photograph in December 1942. The Library of Congress title says it shows locomotives in the roundhouse of the Chicago and North Western railroad at Proviso yard, Chicago, Illinois. Delano was born Yakov Ovcharov in 1914, in the Russian Empire, and later lived much of his life in Puerto Rico. He worked for the Works Progress Administration and the Farm Security Administration, and he was also a composer, filmmaker, cartoonist, poet and professor. The file page does not state how he lit the scene or what film he used, so those details are left out here.
feed.lookAt: Pale light from tall windows at left cuts through smoke or haze, falling across a brick floor, while a small fire glows orange in a barrel. The big locomotive fronts at right stay nearly black. Include one warm light source in a dark space.

caption.title: Locomotives in the roundhouse, Proviso yard

feed.title: Nohkalikai Falls

image.credit: Vikramjit Kakati, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Nohkalikai Falls, sometimes called Ka Likai, is the tallest plunge waterfall in India, dropping 340 metres. It lies in Meghalaya near Cherrapunji, now known as Sohra, one of the wettest places on Earth. The falls are fed by rainwater collected on the summit of a comparatively small plateau, so they lose power in the dry season, from December to February. Below them is a plunge pool of an unusual shade of green. The file page dates this aerial view to 16 April 2021 and credits a team handling photogrammetry, navigation and equipment support.
feed.lookAt: From above the rim, the fall is a thin white thread against a dark, layered cliff, ending in a small turquoise pool. Forest on both sides frames it. The tiny bright pool and the long line toward it show how height reads when something small sits at the end.

feed.title: Elephant Stables, Hampi

image.credit: iMahesh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Hampi, also called the Group of Monuments at Hampi, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Karnataka, India. It was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire from 1336 to 1565, when it was abandoned. A coalition of Muslim sultanates conquered and destroyed the city in 1565, and Hampi remained in ruins. The Elephant Stables are a series of interconnected domed chambers with Indo-Islamic architectural elements, built to house royal elephants. This panorama, taken on 23 September 2024, shows the full length of the structure, emphasising its symmetry and scale, and the grand design reflects how important the royal elephants were to the Vijayanagara Empire.
feed.lookAt: A long row of arched openings and domes spreads across the frame in strict symmetry, with a taller central block, under a pale grey sky. Stand square on and level the horizon. Repeating shapes of the same size reward a panoramic crop.

feed.title: Terraced fields and a road, China

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein made this aerial photograph in 1946 over a mountainous region of China. The Library of Congress title places it in the Kiangsu Province or Yunnan Province and mentions a military vehicle on the road. The Commons file page notes that the long title was written by library staff, because the original gelatin print probably bore only a date. It is held under reproduction number LC-DIG-ppmsca-07414. Rothstein was an American photographer born in 1915. His career spanned five decades, and he was recognised as one of America's premier photojournalists. He died in 1985.
feed.lookAt: A pale road curls down through the centre of the frame between stepped terraces, and a cloudy sky tops the hills. The curve of the road threads the eye through the curved fields. Shoot from above to turn a landscape into a pattern.

caption.title: Terraced fields and a road, China

feed.title: Cholatse

image.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Cholatse, also known as Jobo Lhaptshan, is a mountain in the Khumbu region of the Nepalese Himalaya. Its name is Tibetan for lake pass peak. A long ridge joins it to Taboche, and the Chola glacier descends its east face. It was first climbed by the southwest ridge on 22 April 1982 by Vern Clevenger, Galen Rowell, John Roskelley, Bill O'Connor and Peter Hackett; its north face was first climbed in 1984. This photograph, made on 18 October 2009 from the Chola Valley at about 5,100 metres, shows Cholatse on the right and Ama Dablam on the left, in good weather with high cirrus cloud.
feed.lookAt: Two big peaks stand on either side of a pale glacial lake, and brown rock in the foreground leads the eye down the valley. Put dark rock near the lens and the snow peaks beyond, so the mountains' scale is judged against the valley they rise from.

feed.title: Bou Inania Madrasa

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Bou Inania Madrasa in Fez, Morocco, was built in 1350–55 by the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris. It is the only madrasa in Morocco that also functioned as a congregational mosque, and it is widely seen as a high point of Marinid architecture. The courtyard is surrounded by galleries and flanked by two classroom chambers and a wide prayer hall. Much of the building is covered in carved stucco, zellij tilework and carved wood. This photograph, taken on 3 November 2025, shows the prayer hall and mihrab; the file notes restorations in the 17th, 18th and 20th centuries.
feed.lookAt: A carved arch frames a second arch and the mihrab beyond, with tilework in the foreground edges, forming a tunnel of patterns. Frame deep spaces through their own arches, and keep verticals straight so the symmetry stays calm.

feed.title: Absinthe House entrance, New Orleans

image.credit: Arnold Genthe, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arnold Genthe photographed the entrance of the Absinthe House in New Orleans at some point between 1920 and 1926, according to the Library of Congress, which holds the negative. Genthe was a German-American photographer, born in 1869, and died in 1942. He is best known for his photographs of Northern California, San Francisco's Chinatown and the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, as well as his portraits of politicians, socialites, literary figures and entertainment celebrities. The negative is held by the Library of Congress. The file page gives no further details of this exposure.
feed.lookAt: A pair of arched wooden doors with iron straps stand square in the frame, below a curled iron balcony. Peeling plaster and loose wires add age. Face a doorway straight on, and let the worn wall surface do the storytelling.

feed.title: Zabriskie Point

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Zabriskie Point is part of the Amargosa Range, east of Death Valley in Death Valley National Park, California. It is noted for its erosional landscape, in which water and weather have carved the soft sediments into gullies and ridges. The point is made of sediments from Furnace Creek Lake, which dried up five million years ago, long before Death Valley came into existence. This photograph, taken on 24 December 2013, shows the peak the file calls the Red Cathedral, a banded red-brown cliff above a field of eroded ridges and gullies.
feed.lookAt: Low sidelight picks out every fold in the badlands, while the red cliff above glows against a pale blue sky. A long lens flattens the ridges into stacked bands. Shoot such textured ground when the sun is low, and use the shadows to show the shape.

feed.title: Kotor and the Bay of Kotor

image.credit: Ggia, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kotor is a town on the coast of Montenegro, set in a secluded part of the Bay of Kotor, one of the most indented parts of the Adriatic Sea. It has 13,347 people. The old Mediterranean port is surrounded by fortifications built in the Venetian period, and the town is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Nearly overhanging limestone cliffs rise above the bay. This photograph, taken on 19 July 2009 at 16:58, shows the church of Our Lady of Health, or Crkva Gospa od Zdravlja, above the rooftops, with the bay behind.
feed.lookAt: From a high vantage the church's stone tower stands at right, rooftops in the middle, and the dark bay and mountains fill the distance. The high viewpoint sorts foreground, town and landscape into clear layers. Climb for a view that explains a place.

caption.title: Kotor and the Bay of Kotor

feed.title: Lodgepole Pines, Lyell Fork of the Merced River

image.credit: Ansel Adams, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams made Lodgepole Pines, Lyell Fork of the Merced River. The file page dates the picture to 1921 and says it is part of the Parmelian Prints of the High Sierras portfolio, published by Grabhorn Press in San Francisco in 1927. Adams was given his first camera at the age of 14 during his first visit to Yosemite National Park, and he developed his early work as a member of the Sierra Club. Later he was contracted by the United States Department of the Interior to photograph national parks. The file gives no further information about the day or the exposure.
feed.lookAt: Tall, slim pines rise in dark vertical lines, with sunlit boulders and grass catching the light behind a still, dark pool in the foreground. The pool mirrors the trunks. Look for dark water to repeat a vertical rhythm and balance bright and shaded areas.

caption.title: Lodgepole Pines, Lyell Fork of the Merced River

feed.title: Lake Sylvester, Kahurangi National Park

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kahurangi National Park, in the northwest of New Zealand's South Island, is the country's second largest national park. It was gazetted in 1996 and covers 5,193 km², from the Buller River near Murchison to the base of Farewell Spit. Its geology is the most diverse of any protected area in New Zealand and includes the best sequence of Palaeozoic rocks in the country. The park holds 80% of the country's alpine plant species and about 18 endemic bird species. This photograph of Lake Sylvester at sunrise was taken at 05:08 on 1 January 2020, near Iron Lake, looking towards Nelson.
feed.lookAt: A pink and orange dawn sky lights a small pale lake while blue ridges recede to the horizon in fading layers. The dark rocky foreground anchors the frame. Arrive before sunrise, include the lake as a mirror for the sky, and let the ridges layer.

feed.title: Crystal Mill

image.credit: John Fowler, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Crystal Mill, or the Old Mill, is a wooden powerhouse built in 1892 on an outcrop above the Crystal River in Crystal, Colorado. It is reached from Marble, Colorado, by four-wheel drive. Although it is called a watermill, it is more correctly a compressor station: a water turbine drove an air compressor, and the compressed air powered other machinery or tools. It was originally built with a horizontal wheel. This photograph was taken on 19 September 2012 at 17:43, with the river blurred into a pale ribbon below the mill.
feed.lookAt: The river is smoothed by a long exposure into a white ribbon that curves around grey rock toward the weathered wooden mill perched on its ledge. Autumn aspens glow behind. Use a slow shutter on moving water and place a solid subject above it.

feed.title: Rock & Roll sign, Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith photographed the Rock & Roll sign at the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk, in California, on 9 June 2012. The Library of Congress notes say Santa Cruz was chartered in 1866 and lies on the northern edge of Monterey Bay, about 72 miles south of San Francisco. The picture belongs to the Jon B. Lovelace Collection of California Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, a gift to the Library of Congress in 2012. Highsmith is an American photographer whose nationwide study of the country's landscapes and architecture began in the 1980s.
feed.lookAt: The red, orange and yellow bulb letters spell the sign above a chrome-grilled car, painted rock stars and a blue sky. Colour carries the picture. Shoot signs against a plain, clear sky and crop tight so the bright shapes fill the frame.

caption.title: Rock & Roll sign, Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Fjortende Julibreen

image.credit: AWeith, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Fjortende Julibreen is a glacier in Haakon VII Land on Spitsbergen, Svalbard. It is about sixteen kilometres long and covers about 127 km², reaching down to Fjortende Julibukta in Krossfjorden. It is named after the French national day, 14 July. The glacier lies between Reppingen, Løvlandfjellet and Mercantonfjellet to the south, and Casimir-Périerkammen, Forelryggen and Foreltinden to the north. This photograph, taken on 27 July 2015, shows black-legged kittiwakes, Rissa tridactyla. About 270,000 pairs usually breed on Svalbard in summer, and the birds are often found in front of the glaciers, sitting on ice floes and caring for their plumage during the moult.
feed.lookAt: A dozen kittiwakes sit across a pale blue ice block, in front of the grey, cracked face of the glacier. The birds give scale to the ice. Wait for a small group to settle, then frame them against a plain, textured background.

feed.title: New Sarawak State Legislative Assembly Building

image.credit: Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: North bank of the Sarawak River

feed.story: The New Sarawak Legislative Assembly Building is the state legislative complex of Sarawak, in Kuching, Malaysia. It houses the Sarawak Legislative Assembly, where state assemblymen from across Sarawak meet to debate and pass laws. The complex stands on the north bank of the Sarawak River, between the Astana, the official residence of the state governor, and Fort Margherita. It was officially opened on 27 July 2009 by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Tuanku Mizan Zainal Abidin of Terengganu, followed by the Rulers' Conference. This photograph was taken on 16 July 2017 from across the river.
feed.lookAt: A tall pointed roof tops a tiered building, seen across brown river water and a green lawn, with a small boat crossing the foreground. Water gives you a clear foreground and a view of the whole building. Include a moving boat for scale and life.

caption.title: New Sarawak State Legislative Assembly Building

feed.title: The Flatirons

image.credit: Jesse Varner, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Flatirons are rock formations near Boulder, Colorado, in the western United States. Five large numbered Flatirons run from north to south along the east slope of Green Mountain, which rises to 8,148 ft. The rocks are between 290 and 296 million years old. They are a popular rock-climbing location, with 1,427 routes listed, and many people gather at Chautauqua Park at their base. They serve as the city's signature backdrop and an iconic symbol of Boulder. This wide view is titled winter sunrise and the file dates it to 6 January 2005.
feed.lookAt: The tilted slabs step across the frame in a diagonal row, rose-lit against a clear blue sky, with snowy pines below. A wide crop suits a long row of similar shapes. Look for repeated angles, and shoot when low sun warms the rock.

feed.title: Fuk Tek Kung Temple, Kudat

image.credit: Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kudat is an administrative district in the Malaysian state of Sabah, part of the Kudat Division, which also includes Kota Marudu and Pitas. Kudat Town is the district capital. Fuk Tek Kung Temple, in Kudat, is one of the few Taoist temples in Sabah. According to the file page, it was built in the early 1970s by the nearby Hokkien Association. This photograph was taken on 14 October 2014. It shows the temple's red and yellow tiered roof, topped with dragons, above red pillars, with an incense burner in the courtyard.
feed.lookAt: The temple is shot straight on, with a red and gold roof and curling eaves under a pale sky, its pillars and couplets forming bold vertical bands. A bright, saturated subject suits a flat, frontal view. Keep the camera level so the roofline stays true.

feed.title: Langtang National Park

image.credit: Q-lieb-in, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Langtang National Park lies in north-central Nepal. It was established in 1976 as Nepal's first Himalayan national park and the country's fourth protected area. It covers 1,710 km² across the Nuwakot, Rasuwa and Sindhulpalchok districts and holds 26 village communities and the Langtang valley. The Gosainkunda lake lies at 4,300 m inside the park, and the Dorje Lakpa range, at 6,988 m, bisects it. The summit of Langtang Lirung, at 7,245 m, is its highest point. The park is part of the Sacred Himalayan Landscape. This sunrise view was taken on 13 November 2014 and titled Paints of sunrise.
feed.lookAt: Ridge after ridge stacks up from near-black to pale blue, the farthest layers melting into an orange sky. Haze separates each plane. Use a long lens, expose for the sky, and let the foreground darken so the layers become the subject.

feed.title: Mount Washington Cog Railway

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Mount Washington Cog Railway is the world's first mountain-climbing cog railway. It climbs Mount Washington in New Hampshire, using steam and biodiesel locomotives to carry tourists. It is about 3 miles long, rising from about 2,700 feet above sea level to just short of the summit at 6,288 feet. It is the second-steepest rack railway in the world, after the Pilatus Railway in Switzerland, with an average grade of over 25% and a maximum of 37%. The train climbs at 2.8 miles per hour. This photograph, taken on 7 October 2021, shows the M-7 Kenison ascending.
feed.lookAt: A small orange and purple car climbs a diagonal line of track through gold birches and dark green spruce. The tiny, brightly coloured train is the only warm spot in a sea of yellow. Wait for the moving subject to reach a clean place in the frame.

feed.title: San Pedro de Atacama

image.credit: Luca Galuzzi, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: San Pedro de Atacama is a Chilean town and commune in El Loa Province, Antofagasta Region, some 106 km southeast of Calama and the Chuquicamata copper mine. It overlooks the Licancabur volcano. The town has a significant archaeological museum, the R. P. Gustavo Le Paige museum, and native ruins nearby attract visitors interested in pre-Columbian cultures. Luca Galuzzi photographed these llamas at sunset on 12 April 2006, at an altitude of approximately 2,400 metres in Chile's Norte Grande. The animals graze a pale, dry pasture while the low sun colours the haze along the horizon.
feed.lookAt: Llamas drift across a pale pasture of dry grass while a hazy, golden sky fills the top of the frame. Low sun does the work here. Shoot toward it, expose for the glowing sky, and let the animals' woolly edges pick up warm rim light.

feed.title: Batang County

image.credit: Zhangzhugang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Batang County lies in western Garzê Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan, stretching 260 km from north to south and 45 km from west to east. It borders Tibet across the Jinsha, the upper course of the Yangtze. The low-lying Batang Valley, at about 2,740 metres, is warmer than most of Tibet, and the plain around the town is fertile enough for two harvests a year. The 1990 statistics counted 47,256 people, mostly Tibetans. Zhangzhugang photographed these twin lakes on 16 September 2014 at 17:17, with bare rock peaks and a patch of snow rising behind the water.
feed.lookAt: Two pale lakes, stacked one above the other, lead the eye from a curving road at the bottom up into a wall of rocky peaks and a snowy summit. Look for water that works as a stepping stone, and keep the foreground lake in the frame to give depth.

feed.title: A boat on a river, China

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein (1915 to 1985) was an American photographer whose career spanned five decades, and he is recognised as one of America's premier photojournalists. This photograph of 1946 is titled "A Boat On A River With Rolling Hills In The Background In The Kiangsu Province Or Yunnan Province In China". The Library of Congress holds it as reproduction number LC-DIG-ppmsca-07797, and the version on Commons is a restored copy with mild contrast, tonal adjustments and a final sepia tone. A single sailing junk, its sails raised, sits on glassy water that doubles the dark hills and the pale sky.
feed.lookAt: A lone junk with raised sails sits on glassy water, and its reflection stretches under dark hills. A warm sepia tone unifies the sky and water. Keep the horizon low, and put the boat off-centre so the mirror image carries the lower half.

caption.title: A boat on a river, China

feed.title: Carbajal Valley

image.credit: Godot13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Carbajal Valley is a valley in the Fuegian Andes of southern Tierra del Fuego Province, Argentina. It is approximately 20 kilometres long and runs west to east between the Alvear range to the north and the Vinciguerra range to the south. Peaks in the region are generally lower than 1,250 metres above sea level. Argentine Route 3 runs diagonally through Ushuaia along the Río Olivia and around the base of Mount Olivia. Godot13 took this aerial view on 1 January 2016, looking along the valley's terminus, where braided streams and dark wetlands spread across the flat valley floor.
feed.lookAt: From above, braided streams and dark ponds spread across a flat valley floor, boxed in by steep, forested slopes and snowy peaks. Height turns a landscape into a map. Use a high vantage to show how a river shapes the land, and keep one ridge as your frame.

feed.title: Skjálfandafljót

image.credit: Villy Fink Isaksen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Skjálfandafljót River is in the north of Iceland. At 178 kilometres it is the fourth longest river in the country. It rises at the northwestern border of the Vatnajökull ice cap, runs north parallel to the Sprengisandur highland road and flows into Skjálfandi bay. Along the way it passes many waterfalls, including Aldeyjarfoss and Goðafoss. A team from the University of Sheffield first descended it by kayak in 1989. Villy Fink Isaksen photographed it beside Route 1 on 15 August 2015, where the white water squeezes through a notch in dark rock below grassy banks.
feed.lookAt: White water squeezes through a notch between dark rock banks, with a few tiny visitors on the far ledge for scale. Slow your shutter to blur the foam into silk, or freeze it for texture. Include people only as small, distant markers of size.

feed.title: Rice distribution during famine, China

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein (1915 to 1985) was an American photographer who became one of America's premier photojournalists, and his career spanned five decades. This photograph was taken in 1946 and records the distribution of rice during a time of famine in Jiangsu Province or Yunnan Province in China. It is held by the Library of Congress as ppmsca.07586. The frame is crowded: wide-brimmed straw hats, sacks on the ground and carrying poles bunch beside tiled roofs, and the pale sacks give the eye a bright place to rest in a dark scene.
feed.lookAt: People in wide straw hats crowd between tiled roofs, with pale sacks on the ground and poles on shoulders. A high vantage lets you see the whole gathering. Look for a bright object, here the sacks, and use it to anchor the eye in a busy scene.

feed.title: Nelson Lakes National Park

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Northern end of the Southern Alps

feed.story: Nelson Lakes National Park is in the South Island of New Zealand, at the northern end of the Southern Alps. It was created in 1956, one of four national parks established in the 1950s. The park contains beech forests, multiple lakes, snow-covered mountains and valleys carved by glaciers during the ice ages. Michal Klajban took this picture on 26 July 2019 during sunset in winter. It shows Angelus Hut half buried in snow with Angelus Lake behind it, and an unnamed 1,860-metre peak rising into low cloud above the glowing sky.
feed.lookAt: A tiny hut sits in a huge field of pink-lit snow, with a soft orange sky above the ridge. The small building gives the scene its scale. Wait for sunset light to turn snow pastel, and place a lone structure off-centre so the empty space feels vast.

feed.title: Dyrhólaey

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Dyrhólaey, meaning "door hill island", is a small promontory on the south coast of Iceland, not far from the village of Vík. It was formerly an island of volcanic origin, and the volcano erupted about 100 thousand years ago. The peninsula stands 120 metres high, and a lighthouse built in 1927 sits on top. Off the cliff, a huge black arch of lava stands in the sea, which gave the place its name. Diego Delso photographed the arch on 17 August 2014 with the blue sea showing through the opening and the horizon sitting high.
feed.lookAt: A dark cliff curves out toward the sea, and a natural arch frames a patch of bright turquoise water. The diagonal edge of the cliff leads your eye to the opening. Look for holes and arches that frame a second colour, and keep the horizon level.

feed.title: Flock in Owens Valley

image.credit: Ansel Adams, U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams (1902 to 1984) was an American landscape photographer and environmentalist known for his black-and-white images of the American West. He helped found Group f/64, which championed sharp focus and the full tonal range of a photograph, and with Fred Archer he developed the Zone System, a way of planning tone from exposure through printing. He was contracted by the United States Department of the Interior to photograph national parks. This 1941 picture, "Flock in Owens Valley", is held at the National Archives. A packed mass of sheep fills the lower two thirds, with a low, bare ridge and distant peaks above.
feed.lookAt: A packed sea of sheep fills most of the frame, and the thin line of a bare ridge and far peaks sits above. Repetition gives the picture its texture. Go low and wide, fill the frame with the pattern, and leave a narrow band of sky for calm.

feed.title: Lake Willoughby

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Third best lake in New England (Yankee, 2010)

feed.story: Lake Willoughby is a glacial lake in the town of Westmore in Orleans County, in the Northeast Kingdom of Vermont. The southern end of the lake is surrounded by Willoughby State Forest, which includes Mount Pisgah and Mount Hor, together called Willoughby Gap. In 2010 Yankee magazine named the lake the third best in New England. A public beach lies on the north shore near the outlet, and the village of Westmore sits on the east side where Mill Creek drains Long Pond. King of Hearts took this drone view on 6 October 2021, with Mount Hor on the left and Mount Pisgah on the right.
feed.lookAt: From a drone, the dark blue lake slices between two steep walls of red, orange and yellow forest. Contrast carries the picture. Shoot autumn colour when it peaks, and use a high vantage so the water forms a bold, simple shape among the leaves.

feed.title: Lake Sherburne

image.credit: GlacierNPS (National Park Service), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Bureau of Reclamation's Milk River Project

feed.story: Lake Sherburne is a reservoir in the Many Glacier region of Glacier National Park, Montana. Its dam was built between 1914 and 1921 on Swiftcurrent Creek, flooding six miles of natural lakes and riparian wetlands. It is the main water store of the Bureau of Reclamation's Milk River Project, which irrigates farms in north central Montana. The lake takes its name from Joseph H. Sherburne, who settled near Browning in 1896. This National Park Service panorama looks west-southwest toward Grinnell Point, taken on 7 May 2015, with snowy peaks mirrored in the still water.
feed.lookAt: A very wide panorama lets a line of snowy peaks and their mirror image sit in a thin strip across the middle. Calm water doubles the mountains. Go out early, before the wind, and crop to a long, thin frame so the reflection gets equal weight.

feed.title: Monolith, the Face of Half Dome
feed.collection: Parmelian Prints of the High Sierras

image.credit: Ansel Adams, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams (1902 to 1984) was given his first camera at 14, during his first visit to Yosemite National Park, and developed his early work as a member of the Sierra Club. "Monolith, the Face of Half Dome" is a gelatin silver print of 1927 from the Parmelian Prints of the High Sierras portfolio, published by Grabhorn Press in San Francisco in 1927. In the print, the sheer granite face rises as a dark wall against a black sky, while white snow in the corners makes the rock appear even darker and more massive.
feed.lookAt: A sheer, dark rock face rises against a nearly black sky, with bright snow in the corners. Deep tones add weight. Expose for the highlights so the snow holds detail, and let the sky and shadows stay rich and heavy.

caption.title: Monolith, the Face of Half Dome
caption.line2: Ansel Adams · Parmelian Prints of the High Sierras

feed.title: Darcha

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Darcha is a pair of villages on the Bhaga River in the Lahaul sub-division of Lahaul and Spiti district, in the Indian state of Himachal Pradesh. At 3,360 metres it is the northernmost permanent settlement in the state along the Manali-Leh Highway. The opening of the Atal Tunnel connected it to Manali throughout the year, and a new road toward Padum is under construction. Timothy A. Gonsalves took this picture on 2 June 2024 from above Gemur Gompa, looking upstream along the Bhaga from Jispa to Darcha, with peaks of 5,200 to 5,700 metres beyond.
feed.lookAt: A thin river winds along a narrow valley floor between steep, dark slopes, and snowy peaks fill the far end of the frame. Frame a long valley between two foreground slopes, so the walls lead into the distance and the peaks feel high.

feed.title: Donner Pass

image.credit: Frank Schulenburg, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Donner Pass is a 7,056-foot mountain pass in the northern Sierra Nevada, above Donner Lake and about nine miles west of Truckee, California. Like the Sierra Nevada itself, it has a steep approach from the east and a gradual one from the west. The California Trail, the first transcontinental railroad, the Lincoln Highway and later U.S. Route 40 all used it. It is named for the Donner Party, who overwintered there in 1846. Frank Schulenburg photographed Donner Lake from the pass in July 2013, with forested ridges rolling down to the water and a bright cloud bank on the horizon.
feed.lookAt: Forested ridges roll down to a small lake, and a bright, flat band of cloud closes the top of the frame. A long panorama suits a broad view. Stand on a high point, level the camera, and let the layers of ridges build depth toward the water.

feed.title: View from the Washington Monument, facing west

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith, born in 1946, is an American photographer and author whose decades-long nationwide study documents the landscapes, architecture and people of the United States. She has donated her photographs to the Library of Congress since 1992, a collection of nearly 100,000 images, all in the public domain. This aerial view, taken on 30 April 2007 from the Washington Monument, looks west over the Lincoln Memorial and the National World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C. A long pool runs straight through the middle, flanked by trees, with a river bending beyond.
feed.lookAt: A long reflecting pool runs straight to a distant memorial, with trees and a river bending beyond it. A high vantage organises a city into lines. Pick a tall viewpoint, align the main axis with the centre of the frame, and let the long perspective show the plan.

caption.title: View from the Washington Monument, facing west
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Batu Caves

image.credit: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Batu Caves are a series of limestone caves in Gombak, Selangor, Malaysia, on a 325-metre mogote about 13 kilometres north of Kuala Lumpur. The complex holds many Hindu temples, the most popular of which is a shrine to Murugan, and it is the focal point of the Tamil Hindu festival of Thaipusam in Malaysia. A 43-metre statue of Murugan, among the tallest in the world, stands beside the entrance. CEphoto, Uwe Aranas photographed the statue on 7 May 2015, looking down from above so the gold figure fills the middle of the frame beside the long staircase.
feed.lookAt: A gold statue stands against a red-striped staircase and a green limestone cliff, with tiny climbers showing its size. Bold colour blocks make the design. Choose a high angle so the stairs run through the frame, and wait for people to give scale.

feed.title: Corpus Christi College, Cambridge

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Guild of Corpus Christi and Guild of the Blessed Virgin Mary

feed.story: Corpus Christi College, often shortened to Corpus, is a constituent college of the University of Cambridge. It was established in 1352 by the Guild of Corpus Christi and the Guild of the Blessed Virgin Mary, making it the sixth-oldest college in Cambridge and the only one founded by townspeople. From the late fourteenth century to the early nineteenth it was also commonly known as Bene't College. It has around 300 undergraduates and 200 postgraduates. Diliff photographed New Court on 22 July 2014, a symmetrical panorama of the Gothic frontage above a lawn mown in bold stripes.
feed.lookAt: A symmetrical Gothic front sits above a lawn mown in wide stripes that lead the eye to the central door. Stand on the centre line, keep the camera level, and let the stripes form leading lines. Symmetry works best when nothing tilts.

feed.title: Working on a locomotive, 40th Street shops, Chicago

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano (1914 to 1997) was born Yakov Ovcharov and became an American photographer, filmmaker and composer who spent much of his life in Puerto Rico. In the United States he worked for the Works Progress Administration and, most notably, the Farm Security Administration. In December 1942 he made this colour transparency, titled "C & NW RR [i.e. Chicago and North Western railroad], working on a locomotive at the 40th Street railroad shops, Chicago, Ill." It is held by the Library of Congress. The black locomotive sits in a dim hall, while sun from the tall windows lays bright, gridded patches on the floor.
feed.lookAt: A dark locomotive rests in a dim hall, and sun from tall windows lays gridded, bright patches across the floor. Window light makes shapes. Expose for the lit floor, let the shadows sink, and wait for a worker to stand in a lit patch.

caption.title: Working on a locomotive, 40th Street shops, Chicago

feed.title: Tomb of Hafez

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Tomb of Hafez, known as Hāfezieh, is two memorial structures at the northern edge of Shiraz, Iran, built in memory of the celebrated Persian poet Hafez. The open pavilions stand in the Musalla Gardens on the north bank of a seasonal river and house the marble tomb. The present buildings date from 1935 and were designed by the French architect and archaeologist André Godard, on the site of earlier structures, the best known of which was built in 1773. Diego Delso photographed the pavilion on 24 September 2016 using high dynamic range, looking straight up into its tiled dome.
feed.lookAt: Looking straight up, an eight-sided dome of turquoise and gold tile spirals out from a small round opening, framed by blue sky. Turn the camera to the ceiling. Stand under the centre, keep the frame square and let the pattern's symmetry do the work.

feed.title: Khor Virap

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Khor Virap, "deep dungeon", is an Armenian monastery in the Ararat Plain, near the border with Turkey, about eight kilometres south of Artashat on the site of ancient Artaxata. Gregory the Illuminator, patron saint of Armenia, was imprisoned there for years by King Tiridates III, and in 301 Armenia became the first country to declare itself Christian. Nerses III the Builder built a chapel in 642, and the larger St. Astvatsatsin chapel followed in 1662. Diego Delso photographed it on 1 October 2016, with the monastery on its hill and snowy Mount Ararat filling a clear blue sky behind it.
feed.lookAt: A small stone monastery sits on a brown hill, and a huge snowy peak towers behind it under a clean blue sky. Place a small foreground subject against a large background to show scale. A clear day and a longer lens make the mountain loom.

feed.title: Ore docks and a lake freighter, Cleveland

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano (1914 to 1997), born Yakov Ovcharov, worked for the Farm Security Administration and was also a composer, filmmaker, cartoonist and professor. In May 1943 he made this colour transparency, titled "Pennsylvania R.R. ore docks, unloading ore from a lake freighter by means of 'Hulett' unloaders, Cleveland, Ohio". It is held by the Library of Congress. The dark hull of the freighter, a rust-brown ship with a white pilot house, fills the left side, while a heavy steel unloader leans over the railway tracks that curve toward the viewer.
feed.lookAt: A rust-brown ship hull on the left and a heavy steel crane on the right are joined by railway tracks that curve toward you. Heavy industry is full of strong lines. Stand on the tracks, use their curve as a lead-in, and keep the ship and crane balanced.

caption.title: Ore docks and a lake freighter, Cleveland

feed.title: Neak Pean

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Neak Pean, "the entwined serpents", is an artificial island with a Mahayana Buddhist temple at Angkor, Cambodia. It stands on a circular island in the Jayatataka Baray and was associated with Preah Khan, built during the reign of Jayavarman VII in the 12th century. It is the "Mebon" of the Preah Khan baray. Diego Delso photographed the way across the pond on 17 August 2013. A wooden walkway runs between trees standing in floodwater, and the shade is broken by sun that falls across the planks in long, narrow stripes.
feed.lookAt: A narrow wooden walkway runs straight into the distance between flooded trees, with dappled sun across the planks. A path is a ready-made leading line. Stand in the centre, wait for light to break through the leaves, and let the path vanish toward the temple.

feed.title: Nazca lines

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Nazca lines are a group of geoglyphs in the Nazca Desert of southern Peru, created between 500 BC and 500 AD. People removed the top layer of reddish-brown pebbles to reveal the yellow-grey subsoil, leaving lines typically 10 to 15 centimetres deep. Their combined length is more than 1,300 kilometres. Some figures are best seen from the air, at around 500 metres. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994. Diego Delso took this aerial view of the Monkey on 29 July 2015, with the spiral tail and long limbs drawn in one continuous line.
feed.lookAt: From the air, a single thin line loops into a spiral and forms limbs on pale desert ground. Some subjects only make sense from far above. Fly high and shoot straight down so the ground becomes a flat canvas for the pattern.

feed.title: Cottonwood Trunks, Yosemite Valley

image.credit: Ansel Adams, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams (1902 to 1984) first visited Yosemite National Park at the age of 14, when he was given his first camera, and he went on to become one of America's best-known landscape photographers. He co-founded Group f/64, which favoured sharp focus and the full range of tones. This 1932 photograph, "Cottonwood Trunks, Yosemite Valley", is a black-and-white study of tall, pale trunks that lean and twist against a dark background of forest. The smooth bark glows against the shadow, and the curves of the trunks give the picture its movement.
feed.lookAt: Pale, smooth trunks lean and twist against dark forest shadows, and one long curve sweeps across the frame. Look past the whole tree to its parts. Fill the frame with a few trunks, expose for the bright bark, and let the dark background isolate them.

feed.title: Gamlehaugen

image.credit: Aqwis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Gamlehaugen is a Royal Castle in Bergen, Norway, and the residence of the Norwegian royal family in the city. Its history goes back to the Middle Ages, and past owners include some of the wealthiest men in Bergen. The politician and shipping magnate Christian Michelsen, later the first prime minister of Norway after the union with Sweden ended, commissioned the current main building. When he died in 1925, a national fund-raising campaign raised enough money for the state to buy the property. Aqwis photographed it on 24 June 2008, with the white tower and its dark pointed roof beside a large tree.
feed.lookAt: A white tower with a dark pointed roof stands beside a huge leafy tree, with a green lawn rolling into the corner of the frame. Use a tree as one side of the frame, and shoot on a day with white clouds so the building stays bright against the sky.

feed.title: Atomium

image.credit: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Atomium is a modernist landmark in Brussels, Belgium, built as the centrepiece of the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. The engineer André Waterkeyn and the architects André and Jean Polak designed it as a tribute to scientific progress. It stands 102 metres tall, and its nine stainless-steel-clad spheres, each 18 metres across, are arranged as an iron crystal's unit cell magnified 165 billion times. Trougnouf photographed the central sphere on 5 October 2018, looking up from below, where its mirror-like surface reflects the base and the Osseghem park against a blue sky.
feed.lookAt: A mirror-bright sphere hangs against deep blue sky, and its surface bends the ground and base into a tiny curved scene. Shoot reflective surfaces from a low angle so the sky stays clean, and look for the world folded inside the curve.

feed.title: Near White Plains, Georgia

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano (1914 to 1997) was born Yakov Ovcharov in the Russian Empire and became an American photographer who worked most notably for the Farm Security Administration. This colour transparency, titled "Near White Plains, Ga., ca. 1941", is held by the Library of Congress, where it is catalogued under Delano and Marion Post Wolcott. It shows a weathered wooden building standing alone among trees, with a flag hung from the upper doorway and a figure on the sunlit ground in front. The washed-out colours and the pale sky are typical of early colour slides.
feed.lookAt: A weathered wooden building stands alone among dark trees, with a flag at the upper door and a person at the foot. Centre a solitary subject and let the empty space around it speak. A small figure at the base gives scale and a human anchor.

feed.title: Gangneung

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Gangneung is a municipal city in South Korea's Gangwon province, on the east coast. It is the economic centre of the Yeongdong region and had 213,658 residents in 2017. Jeongdongjin, a popular spot for watching the sunrise, and Gyeongpo Beach are among its attractions. The city hosted all the ice events at the 2018 Winter Olympics and the 2024 Winter Youth Olympics. Basile Morin photographed colourful clouds mirrored in the Namdae stream from the Wolhwagyo bridge on 8 June 2024, during the Gangneung Danoje celebration, with rows of lights along the far bank.
feed.lookAt: Pink and gold clouds reflect in a calm stream, with the city's lights glowing along the far bank. Wait for dusk, when the sky and the water match in brightness. Shoot from a bridge, hold steady, and let the reflection carry half the picture.

feed.title: Ardez

image.credit: Agnes Monkelbaan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ardez is a former municipality in the district of Inn in the canton of Graubünden, in eastern Switzerland, in the Lower Engadin valley.
